paper: Jurrus et al. 2018 (Protein Science 27:112-128) — Improvements to the APBS biomolecular solvation software suite
context: This replication exercised the FD-multigrid path (MG-auto, LPBE) on Born ion, methanol/methoxide regression tests, and 1AKI lysozyme. It did NOT exercise nonlinear PBE, TABI-PB boundary elements, geometric-flow non-polar solvation, or GPU/MD-coupled workflows. The five questions below are open in that gap.

open_questions.q: Does the nonlinear Poisson-Boltzmann (NPBE) solver in APBS converge robustly for highly-charged biomolecules (e.g. B-DNA duplexes, ribosomal fragments, polyanionic membranes) without heuristic damping, and how does the multigrid Newton loop scale with net charge density and grid resolution?
open_questions.basis: The replication used only LPBE inputs; the paper advertises improvements relevant to highly-charged systems (nucleic acids, membranes) where LPBE is known to break down and NPBE must be used. Nothing in the reproduced regression tests (Born ion, methanol/methoxide, 1AKI) stresses the nonlinear branch. The Newton-multigrid convergence behavior of APBS on charge densities |sigma| >~ 1 e/nm^2 is not characterized in this replication.
next_steps: Build a graded test suite of increasing charge density: single ion -> methanol -> lysozyme -> 20-bp B-DNA duplex -> a POPS lipid patch.
Run each with npbe under mg-auto, log Newton iteration counts, residual histories, and any 'nonconvergent' flags.
Compare fine-grid NPBE energies to LPBE at matched geometry to quantify where the linearization error exceeds 1 kT.

open_questions.q: What is the quantitative gap between APBS continuum-PBE polar solvation free energies and explicit-solvent (TIP3P/OPC) free-energy-perturbation reference values on a common small-molecule benchmark (e.g. the Mobley FreeSolv set)?
open_questions.basis: The paper's replicated tests are self-consistent (regression numbers reproduce to 6+ decimals) but never compare against explicit-solvent MD. The 1AKI number here (~-4300 kJ/mol) is 'physically reasonable' but not anchored to any MD/FEP reference. The community-relevant question — how faithful is PBE as an implicit-solvent model — is not addressed by either the paper or this replication.
next_steps: Run APBS (LPBE + NPBE) on the FreeSolv 642-molecule set with a fixed parameter recipe (pdie=1, sdie=78.54, srad=1.4, sdens=10).
Compare to published FreeSolv TIP3P FEP numbers; report mean signed error, MAE, RMSE, R^2.
Break the residual down by chemical class (neutral vs charged, polar vs apolar) to identify where the continuum picture systematically fails.

open_questions.q: How much accuracy is gained (or lost) by APBS's adaptive / focused mesh strategies (MG-auto multi-level focusing, and the finite-element bcx path) versus a uniform grid at matched wall-clock cost on protein-scale systems?
open_questions.basis: This replication used MG-auto at dime=129^3 and 161^3 on 1AKI and observed a ~2% gap between the two levels — a normal but non-trivial discretization signature. Whether the paper's touted mesh-adaptivity actually delivers a better accuracy/cost frontier than a plain uniform grid, or than a Richardson extrapolation of two coarse grids, was not measured here.
next_steps: On 1AKI and a larger test protein (e.g. barnase), sweep MG-auto grid levels 65^3, 97^3, 129^3, 161^3, 193^3; fit Richardson extrapolation to obtain a converged reference.
Repeat with the finite-element solver on the same geometry at matched DoF count and matched wall-clock.
Plot |E_solv(N) - E_ref| vs wall-clock; identify whether MG-auto, FE, or Richardson-of-uniform wins the Pareto frontier.

open_questions.q: Is there a validated GPU-accelerated implementation of the APBS multigrid PBE solver that matches CPU MG-auto numerics to within regression tolerance while delivering an actual speedup, and if so on which hardware family?
open_questions.basis: The paper's era (v1.5, 2017/2018) predates GPU-first PBE work; this replication ran a CPU multigrid only. The paper does not claim a GPU backend, but the software's forward roadmap and the availability of A100-class hardware on uicgpu make the presence/absence of a validated GPU path an open, replication-adjacent question.
next_steps: Survey the APBS 3.x source tree and issue tracker for any CUDA/HIP/SYCL solver branches; document status (merged, experimental, dead).
If a GPU branch exists, build it against the same conda env; run the same born/solv regression suite and record bitwise-vs-tolerance-vs-fail per test.
Benchmark wall-clock on 1AKI 161^3 CPU (24-core) vs GPU (A100) to quantify any real speedup, not just a per-iter FLOP claim.

open_questions.q: How stable are APBS-derived polar solvation energies along an MD trajectory (single-conformation vs snapshot-averaged), and does the choice of conformational ensemble change the ranking of tested variants (e.g. WT vs mutant protein, or apo vs holo)?
open_questions.basis: This replication computed PBE energies on a single crystallographic conformation of 1AKI. Real applications (electrostatic contributions to binding affinity, pKa shifts, alchemical corrections) require ensemble averages over MD-generated conformations. The single-snapshot vs trajectory-mean gap, and its variance, is not characterized here or in the paper's own benchmarks.
next_steps: Run a short (10-50 ns) MD trajectory of 1AKI in explicit water; extract 100 evenly-spaced snapshots.
Run APBS MG-auto polar solvation on each snapshot; report mean, stddev, and time-decorrelated error bar.
Repeat for a WT-vs-mutant pair (e.g. T4 lysozyme L99A) and check whether the mutant/WT rank order flips between single-conformation and ensemble-averaged PBE.
